audit_records.rationale: {"kind": "briefing", "translation_id": "tr.ps027.0001", "briefing": {"psalm_id": "ps027", "translation_id": "tr.ps027.0001", "background": {"authorship": "The Hebrew heading is simply לְדָוִד, associating the psalm with David without naming an occasion. Its wording can indicate authorship, dedication, or membership in a Davidic collection; these possibilities do not establish who composed it. Jewish and Christian tradition commonly understand David as its author. Critical scholarship distinguishes the heading's attribution from independently recoverable authorship. Hermann Gunkel regarded verses 1–6 and 7–14 as originally separate compositions; Peter Craigie and Marvin Tate defended their literary unity through shared vocabulary and themes. Neither position identifies an otherwise unknown author. See the [Faithlife discussion of Davidic headings](https://biblia.com/books/fsb/article/SIDEBAR.DAVIDANDTHEPSALMTITLES) and [Benjamin D. Sommer's discussion of Psalm 27](https://www.thetorah.com/article/a-faith-that-includes-doubt-psalm-27).", "setting": "The text names threatening enemies, warfare, false witnesses, sanctuary worship, and possible parental abandonment, but supplies no date or identifiable historical event. Davidic reconstructions place it roughly in the tenth century BCE. A. F. Kirkpatrick connects at least the opening part with Absalom's rebellion, citing its military language and longing for God's dwelling; the Greek heading instead locates it before an unspecified anointing. These are different proposed settings, not equivalent evidence. [Kirkpatrick's commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/27.htm). Adam Clarke also entertained an exilic setting, understanding the sanctuary longing against displacement, without demonstrating that date. [Clarke's commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/27.htm). Sanctuary-based reconstructions include a threatened worshiper's prayer and thanksgiving, and legal asylum: Benzion Dinur proposed use by someone seeking refuge, while Shalom E. Holtz cautions against making a specific asylum institution explain all the imagery. References to house, temple, shelter, and tent do not by themselves distinguish a Davidic sanctuary, the First Temple, or the Second Temple. [Holtz on refuge and the Temple](https://www.thetorah.com/article/taking-refuge-in-god-beyond-the-temple-walls-psalm-27).", "form": "The psalm combines individual confidence, petition, and anticipated thanksgiving. It has no alphabetic acrostic, Selah, or musical direction beyond the Davidic heading. Its paired clauses, opening rhetorical questions, repeated closing command, and recurring words for seeking, face, heart, salvation, enemies, and life help bind it together. Especially significant is the contrast between God hiding the speaker safely in verse 5 and the plea that God not hide his face in verse 9. Speaking about God in verses 1–6 gives way mainly to speaking directly to God in verses 7–12; the ending returns to testimony and exhortation. Stanza divisions are editorial, and no fixed English meter is prescribed. Greek-source provenance: comparisons use the supplied Greek Psalm 26 in H. B. Swete, The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint, vol. 2 (Cambridge, 1896), Psalms; transcribed from page images by the rahlfs1931-psalter project, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Source IDs: lxx, swete1896; source_version: swete1896:r0001:edda9c613905b0a0161deb0fe7fd5a0a79beda5d0f83fe13cf354f514d3f957e. The supplied mapping is proposed; the Greek alternatives below remain choices for review, not adopted readings.", "themes": "Confidence and vulnerability coexist. Verses 1–3 declare that divine protection outweighs hostile power; verses 4–6 make continuing access to God the speaker's central desire. Verse 7 abruptly introduces urgent petition. Seeking God's face becomes fear of rejection, followed by appeals for welcome, guidance, and protection against accusation. Verse 13 expresses trust through a difficult, unfinished Hebrew construction; verse 14 closes with repeated encouragement to wait or hope. Translating the ending as uninterrupted certainty, suspended speech, or reassurance from another voice changes the psalm's emotional movement. Its threats are worldly and concrete, while its sanctuary imagery also supports broader experiences of divine presence.", "reception": "Many Ashkenazi communities recite the psalm during Elul and the autumn holy days, with different ending dates. This is later liturgical use, not an occasion specified by the psalm. Midrash associates its light with Rosh Hashanah and salvation with Yom Kippur; later interpretation connects its shelter with Sukkot. [Alan Cooper on the custom](https://www.jtsa.edu/torah/psalm-27-the-days-of-awe/). Berakhot 4a reads verse 13's extraordinary dots in relation to David's uncertainty about his own share in future reward. [Berakhot 4a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.4a?lang2=en&with=II+Samuel). Augustine reads the psalm through a Christian believer's struggles and interprets its living land eschatologically. [Augustine's exposition](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801027.htm). Christian worship includes the Anglican monthly Psalter and Catholic Vespers, where the psalm is divided into two parts. [Book of Common Prayer](https://www.churchofengland.org/prayer-and-worship/worship-texts-and-resources/book-common-prayer/psalter/psalms-27-29), [John Paul II on its Vespers use](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/audiences/2004/documents/hf_jp-ii_aud_20040428.html). There is no explicit, introduced New Testament quotation of this psalm. Comparison suggests a possible echo of its Greek courage formula in 1 Corinthians 16:13, although similar language occurs elsewhere in Scripture; thematic connections with Jesus as light or with false witnesses are reception, not proof of quotation.
